questions.q:
Statement I: The Maurya empire broke up only after a long decline lasting well over a century after Ashoka.
Statement II: Every one of the new kingdoms that emerged was founded by a ruler from outside the subcontinent.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Both are false. The chapter says the breakup came hardly half a century after Ashoka, and that many new kingdoms were earlier tributary kingdoms of the Maurya empire, not outsiders.
o: Both statements are false.
Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.

questions.q: Write a short diary entry (three or four lines) by the king of a small kingdom that had paid tribute to the Maurya court, written two years after the assassination of the last emperor. It must show (i) why his kingdom now stands on its own, (ii) one peaceful and one forceful way he might gain control at his border, and (iii) why he cares about that border.
questions.a: A good entry says the empire has broken up so tribute and overlordship have ended and his kingdom is one of the many new kingdoms; he may seek a matrimonial alliance with a neighbour or send soldiers to the border district; and he cares because holding border areas keeps his kingdom safe from attacks.
s: Kingdom stands alone after the breakup
One peaceful and one forceful method of gaining control
Border control keeps the kingdom safe

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A king in this age could strengthen his hold over a border area without fighting a battle.
Reason (R): Matrimonial alliances between neighbouring kingdoms were one of the peaceful methods of gaining control.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: a marriage link between royal families was a peaceful way of gaining control, so a king could secure his border area without war.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rajni's notes on a small kingdom read: 'It paid tribute to the Maurya court for generations. Months after the emperor was assassinated, its king stopped sending tribute and began arranging a marriage link with a neighbour.' Which reading of these notes fits the chapter's account?
questions.a: The chapter says many new kingdoms were earlier tributary kingdoms under Maurya overlordship and that the new kingdoms competed, peacefully by matrimonial alliances or by force. The Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire, not an absorber of provinces, and invaders came later through the weak northwest.
o: A former tributary now acting as a new competing kingdom
A Maurya province being absorbed into a larger Shunga empire
An invader setting up a kingdom through the northwest
A border kingdom surrendering land to buy its safety

questions.q: A student works out the length of the timeline from 200 BCE to 300 CE as 300 - 200 = 100 years. (a) What slip has she made in handling BCE and CE years? (b) What is the correct length and how is it found?
questions.a: (a) She subtracted, but the two ends lie on opposite sides of the BCE/CE change: BCE years count down to 1 BCE and CE years count up from 1 CE, so the two stretches are added. (b) 200 + 300 = 500 years.
s: Slip: subtracted years that lie on opposite sides of BCE and CE
500 years by adding 200 and 300

questions.q: Aman says, 'The new kingdoms of this age were founded by foreign invaders, which is why scholars call it the age of reorganisation.' Is he right? Judge his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. Many of the new kingdoms were earlier tributary kingdoms of the Maurya empire, so they were not foreign. The name refers to existing regions being reorganised into new, competing kingdoms. Invaders came later, through the northwest that had become weak after the breakup.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Many new kingdoms were earlier Maurya tributaries
The name means regions reorganised; invaders came later through the weak northwest

questions.q: In a debate a classmate says, 'With kings busy in marriage deals and wars, this age can have had little art or writing.' Which statement from the chapter is the best reply?
questions.a: The chapter says that together with the political events there was a burst in the development of art, architecture and literature, and enriching cultural exchanges. The other statements are true but say nothing about art or writing.
o: Alongside the political events came a burst in art, architecture and literature
The northwest became weak, which exposed it to invasions from outside the subcontinent
Peaceful methods like matrimonial alliances were used alongside warfare to gain control
Gaining control of border areas was important to keep a kingdom safe from attacks

questions.q: A museum wall is divided into 'dynasties from within the subcontinent' and 'dynasties from outside it'. A volunteer places the Satavahanas on the outside side because their traders sold goods to the Roman Empire. What should the museum do, going by the chapter's own grouping of dynasties?
questions.a: The chapter's grouping lists the Satavahanas with the Shungas, Chedis, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas as dynasties from within the subcontinent. Trade with distant lands does not make a dynasty foreign; the outside group is the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas.
o: Move them inside, beside the Shungas and Chedis
Keep them outside, since their trade reached the Roman Empire
Move them outside, beside the Indo-Greeks, who also issued coins
Put them on a line between the two groups

questions.q:
King Veerasena's treasury holds 40 lakh rupees and he must keep at least 12 lakh for the winter. His neighbour claims a border district that guards Veerasena's own frontier. Plan 1: send his 4,000 soldiers to take the district; the season would cost 22 lakh rupees, and the neighbour has 6,000 soldiers. Plan 2: offer his daughter in marriage into the neighbour's royal family; the gifts and the wedding would cost 28 lakh rupees, the neighbour would promise not to attack the district, and Veerasena would give up one small border village.
(a) What does the chapter call the means each plan uses, and which is peaceful?
(b) How much of the treasury is left under each plan, and does each meet the winter reserve?
(c) Why would the king care so much about the district, according to the chapter?
(d) Which plan would you advise? Use your figures and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Plan 1 uses force in warfare; Plan 2 is a matrimonial alliance, the peaceful method. (b) Plan 1: 40 - 22 = 18 lakh, above the 12-lakh reserve. Plan 2: 40 - 28 = 12 lakh, exactly the reserve. (c) Control of border areas was important to keep the kingdom safe from attacks. (d) Either plan can be defended: Plan 1 is cheaper by 6 lakh and could win the whole district, but his 4,000 face 6,000; Plan 2 leaves no spare money and costs a village but avoids a battle against larger numbers and secures the border.
s: Part (a): force and matrimonial alliance, alliance peaceful
Part (b): 18 lakh and 12 lakh, reserve met by both
Part (c): border areas keep the kingdom safe
Part (d): a plan chosen with figures and the chapter

questions.q: Two kings plan to win control of a neighbour's border area: one by a marriage alliance with the neighbour's royal family, the other by a campaign. (a) Which plan needs the neighbour's agreement before it can work, and why? (b) What does the chapter say both kings are really after?
questions.a: (a) The marriage alliance, because it is an alliance arranged through a marriage between two royal families, so the other family must agree; a campaign does not wait for agreement. (b) Control over the border areas, which was important to keep the kingdom safe from attacks.
s: Marriage alliance, with the reason that it is arranged between two families
Control of border areas to keep the kingdom safe

questions.q: True or False: A kingdom could count among the 'new' kingdoms of this age even though it had already existed earlier under the Maurya emperor's overlordship. Give the reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. The chapter says many new kingdoms emerged across the subcontinent and that they were often earlier tributary kingdoms under Maurya overlordship; 'new' means newly independent after the breakup, not newly founded.
s: The verdict
The reason or correction

questions.q: A class draws a timeline from the first year of the 2nd century BCE to the last year of the 3rd century CE and marks the assassination of the last Maurya emperor at 185 BCE. Counting both end years, the part of the timeline from that mark to its right-hand end covers ___ years.

Some scholars call this period the 'age of reorganisation'. (a) State from the chapter what was being reorganised and what the resulting kingdoms kept doing. (b) Give one fact the name 'age of collapse' would hide.
questions.a: (a) Existing regions were being reorganised into new kingdoms that were constantly competing to become powerful. (b) Any one: there was a burst in art, architecture and literature with enriching cultural exchanges; new kingdoms emerged to fill the gap; the map and people's lives changed significantly.
s: Regions reorganised into new, constantly competing kingdoms
One fact that 'collapse' would hide

questions.q: Differentiate a matrimonial alliance from the use of force as ways of gaining control over an area, stating what each does to the relation between the two kingdoms.
questions.a: A matrimonial alliance is a peaceful method: a marriage between royal families cements an alliance, so the two kingdoms become friendly partners. The use of force is warfare: one kingdom tries to take control by fighting, so the two stay rivals.
s: Alliance: peaceful, cements a tie between the two kingdoms
Force: warfare, the kingdoms remain rivals

questions.q: A student draws four cause-and-effect arrows for the opening of the chapter. Which arrow does the chapter NOT support?
questions.a: The chapter's order is the reverse: the last emperor was assassinated and the empire broke up, and only then did the weakened northwest become exposed to invasions from outside. The other three arrows follow the chapter.
o: Invasions through the northwest, then the breakup of the Maurya empire
The breakup of the empire, then a weak northwest open to invasions
Former tributaries standing alone, then many new kingdoms
Constant competition among new kingdoms, then a changed map of India

questions.q:
Read the statements about the kingdoms of this age.
1. Among the dynasties listed in the chapter's Fig. 6.3, every dynasty except the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas came from outside the subcontinent.
2. A kingdom that had earlier been a tributary under Maurya overlordship could appear among the new kingdoms of this age.
3. A matrimonial alliance would often mean a king offering his daughter in marriage into the royal family of a neighbouring kingdom.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the Shungas, Chedis and Satavahanas are also listed as dynasties from within the subcontinent, so only the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas came from outside. Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The chapter's first Big Question asks why this period is called the 'Age of Reorganisation'. A student writes only: 'Because the empire broke up.' Give three things the answer is missing, using the chapter.
questions.a: It misses that new kingdoms, often earlier tributary kingdoms, emerged; that they were constantly competing, by matrimonial alliances or force, over areas such as borders; and that regions were reorganised so the map of India and people's lives changed.
s: New kingdoms emerged, many of them former tributaries
They competed by marriage alliances or force
Regions were reorganised so the map and lives changed

questions.q: Suppose the last Maurya emperor had not been assassinated and the empire had held together for another century. Using only what the chapter says followed the breakup, predict three things that would probably NOT have happened as they did. Then name the weakest of your three predictions and say why it is weakest.
questions.a: Predictions (any three): many new kingdoms, often former tributaries, would not have emerged; the northwest would not have become weak and open to invasion; competition between kingdoms by marriage alliances or force over borders would not have shaped the map; the Shungas would not have founded their own dynasty. The weakest is the one the chapter only links loosely, for example the burst in art, which the chapter says happened 'together with' the political events without saying they caused it, or invasions, which could have come anyway.
s: First prediction
Second prediction
Third prediction
Names the weakest prediction
Reason it is weakest

questions.q:
A class has one strip of paper, 50 cm long, to draw a timeline from the first year of the 2nd century BCE to the last year of the 3rd century CE (500 years). Labels for two events must be at least 2 cm apart to be readable. Option X: draw at 1 cm for every 10 years on the single strip. Option Y: draw at 1 cm for every 5 years on two 50 cm strips joined together.
(a) How long is the timeline under each option, and how far from the left end is the mark for the assassination of the last Maurya emperor, around 185 BCE (measured from the first year)?
(b) Can the labels for the start of the period and for that assassination be separated by 2 cm under each option?
(c) Who carried out that assassination?
(d) Which option would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) X: 500 / 10 = 50 cm, with the mark 15 / 10 = 1.5 cm from the left end. Y: 500 / 5 = 100 cm, with the mark 15 / 5 = 3 cm from the left end. (b) Under X the gap is 1.5 cm, less than 2 cm, so the labels crowd; under Y it is 3 cm, so they fit. (c) His commander-in-chief, Pushyamitra Shunga. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: Y keeps the two key events readable but needs a join; X fits one strip, but the first two labels would have to be placed one above and one below the line.
s: Part (a): 50 cm and 100 cm; 1.5 cm and 3 cm
Part (b): crowded under X, fits under Y
Part (c): Pushyamitra Shunga, commander-in-chief
Part (d): a choice with a reason that weighs readability against fit

questions.q: Two names are proposed for the period after the Mauryas: 'Age of Breakup' and 'Age of Reorganisation'. Decide which the chapter supports better. Give two points that fit 'Breakup', two points that fit 'Reorganisation', and your conclusion.
questions.a: Breakup: the last emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE; the empire broke up hardly half a century after Ashoka; the northwest became weak and exposed to invasions. Reorganisation: new kingdoms, often former tributaries, emerged; they competed constantly by alliances or force; there was a burst in art, architecture and literature. Conclusion: 'Reorganisation' is better because the breakup was followed by regions being remade into new kingdoms and the map changed; 'breakup' describes only the first step. A reasoned case for the other name is acceptable if it addresses both lists.
s: Two points that fit Breakup
Two points that fit Reorganisation
A conclusion giving a reason

questions.q: A quiz key says: 'The Maurya empire broke up about 200 years after Ashoka.' Using the chapter, show that this cannot be correct.
questions.a: The chapter says the breakup came hardly half a century after Ashoka, so well under 100 years and about 50 at most. 200 years is at least four times as long, so the key contradicts the chapter.
s: Quotes the chapter: hardly half a century after Ashoka
Compares about 50 years with 200 years
Concludes the key is wrong and corrects it

questions.q:
A guide at the Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh tells 36 students of Class 7, 'This stupa was probably built in the time of Ashoka, and a later dynasty then enriched it. All the carvings you see here show only the Buddha's life.' The school has Rs 12,000 for the outing. A bus visit costs Rs 450 per student; a photograph-study session in class, covering every panel, costs Rs 9,000 for all 36.
(a) Which dynasty enriched the stupa, and what did it add?
(b) Why are these additions important for the history of art?
(c) The chapter's picture of the railings shows a carving of Lakshmi, a group of singers and dancers, and elephants holding up the wheel of dharma. Which two are most clearly not about the Buddha's life?
(d) Work out how many students the bus visit can take within Rs 12,000 and compare it with the photograph session. Advise the school, giving one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Shungas; carved railings and reliefs depicting stories from the Buddha's life. (b) They are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art. (c) The carving of Lakshmi and the group of singers and dancers (the wheel of dharma is a Buddhist symbol). (d) 12,000 / 450 = 26.67, so 26 students (26 x 450 = 11,700), 10 fewer than the class; the session reaches all 36 for Rs 9,000. A justified choice is accepted: the session shows every panel to everyone, while the visit shows the real railings to 26.
s: Part (a): Shungas, railings and reliefs
Part (b): earliest examples of Buddhist art
Part (c): Lakshmi and singers and dancers
Part (d): 26 students against all 36, with a justified choice

questions.q: True or False: Because the Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire, the chapter treats Pushyamitra's performance of the ashvamedha yajna as a sign that he ruled a larger area than the Mauryas. Give the reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the ritual was meant to establish him as a most powerful ruler, but his Shunga dynasty ruled over only parts of north and central India and the empire was smaller than the Maurya empire.
s: The verdict
The reason or correction

questions.q: The chapter's collage of Shunga contributions to art (Fig. 6.6) includes a pillar carved with a Greek warrior. Which statement from the chapter makes a Greek figure in Shunga art least surprising?
questions.a: The chapter says Pushyamitra maintained friendly relations with the Greeks after an initial military campaign, which fits a Greek figure appearing in Shunga art. The other statements are true but say nothing about the Greeks.
o: Pushyamitra kept friendly relations with the Greeks after some initial fighting
The Shunga dynasty ruled over parts of north and central India, not the whole subcontinent
The Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh shows some of the earliest Buddhist art
The aśvamedha yajna was a Vedic ritual conducted by many rulers

questions.q: A student's test answer reads: 'Pushyamitra's empire was smaller than the Maurya empire, yet he kept it safe from potential invaders and kept friendly relations with the Greeks after some initial military campaign against them.' Check each part against the chapter and give your verdict on the answer.
questions.a: Yes, all of it. The chapter says the Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire (compare their maps), that he kept it safe from potential invaders, and that he maintained friendly relations with the Greeks after some initial military campaign against them.
s: Verdict: Yes, supported
Smaller than the Maurya empire, and kept safe from invaders
Friendly relations came after an initial military campaign

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Shunga age.
1. Sanskrit emerged as one of the preferred languages for philosophical and literary works in this period.
2. The Bharhut Stupa was built from its foundations by the Shungas, who also carved its first railings.
3. The Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire, yet Pushyamitra kept it safe from potential invaders.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: the stupa was probably built during Ashoka's time and the Shungas added the railings and reliefs. Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A visitor to the Bharhut Stupa says, 'Reviving Vedic rituals and supporting Buddhist art are opposite policies; a ruler can only have chosen one.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter's account of the Shunga age.
questions.a: The statement is not supported. Vedic rituals such as the ashvamedha were revived, but the chapter says other schools of thought continued to flourish. The Shungas patronised literature, art and architecture. Sanskrit was preferred for philosophical and literary works and the Yoga Sutras were compiled. At Bharhut they added railings and reliefs on the Buddha's life, among the earliest examples of Buddhist art, so the two went together.
s: Revival of Vedic rituals, with the ashvamedha as an example
Other schools still flourished
Sanskrit works and the Yoga Sutras
Bharhut railings and reliefs as Buddhist art
Judgement that revival and openness went together

questions.q: The chapter says Pushyamitra assassinated the last Maurya emperor around 185 BCE and that his empire was gone a century later; it also says the Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, south of the Shunga empire, from the 2nd century BCE onward. (a) About when was the Shunga empire gone, and must it have overlapped in time with the Satavahanas? (b) The chapter says the Shungas seem to have waged wars with neighbours, which 'may have included' the Satavahanas. Does it prove the two fought? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 185 - 100 = about 85 BCE. The 2nd century BCE runs from 200 to 101 BCE, so the Satavahanas began some time between 200 and 101 BCE, before the Shunga empire was gone; the two overlapped. (b) No. 'May have included' and 'from the limited evidence available' make it only a possibility.
s: About 85 BCE and an overlap with the 2nd-century BCE start of the Satavahanas
Not proved: 'may have included' on limited evidence

questions.q: (a) An ashvamedha horse returns after a year without having been stopped by anyone. What can the king claim? (b) Why would a king with a weak army hesitate to perform the ritual?
questions.a: (a) All the territory the horse crossed unchallenged is considered part of his empire. (b) Any ruler could stop the horse and that would lead to a battle to determine supremacy, which a king with a weak army might lose.
s: Crossed territory counts as part of his empire
A stopped horse means a battle he might lose

questions.q: Pushyamitra used a ritual (the ashvamedha yajna) and a policy of friendly relations with the Greeks to secure his position. Compare the two as ways of protecting a kingdom: say what each asks of the king, what risk each carries, and which you think served the Shunga empire better, using what the chapter says about the empire's size and how long it lasted.
questions.a: The ritual asks the king to send a horse with soldiers across other lands; its risk is that a ruler stops the horse and a battle must decide supremacy. Friendly relations, kept after an initial campaign, ask for restraint and a settlement with a neighbour; the risk is that peace may not hold. The chapter says the empire was kept safe from potential invaders but was smaller than the Maurya empire and gone a century later. A reasoned judgement is accepted: friendly relations protected the empire, while the ritual declared a claim that the smaller, short-lived empire could not make permanent.
s: What the ritual asks of the king
The ritual's risk
What friendly relations ask and their risk
Outcome the chapter reports: kept safe, smaller, gone in a century
A reasoned judgement

questions.q:
Rajat is making a poster on the Shungas and has four evidence cards: Card 1, the Shunga empire was kept safe from potential invaders; Card 2, friendly relations with the Greeks after an initial campaign; Card 3, carved railings and reliefs added at Bharhut; Card 4, the Yoga Sutras compiled in Sanskrit by Patanjali. He must pick a title: 'Protector of a smaller empire' or 'Patron of art and learning'.
(a) Pushyamitra took power around 185 BCE and the empire was gone a century later. By about which year BCE did it end?
(b) Which two cards fit 'Protector' and which two fit 'Patron'?
(c) What share of the 500-year timeline from 200 BCE to 300 CE does a hundred-year empire cover?
(d) Which title would you choose, using the cards and your answer to (c)?
questions.a: (a) 185 - 100 = about 85 BCE. (b) Protector: Cards 1 and 2. Patron: Cards 3 and 4. (c) 100 / 500 = 20 per cent. (d) Either title can be defended, as the cards split two and two: 'Protector' fits an empire that was smaller and short-lived but kept safe; 'Patron' fits what outlasted the dynasty, the Bharhut reliefs and Sanskrit works, though the patronage belongs to the dynasty and not only to Pushyamitra.
s: Part (a): about 85 BCE
Part (b): Cards 1 and 2 with Protector, Cards 3 and 4 with Patron
Part (c): 20 per cent
Part (d): a title chosen with evidence from the cards and the 20 per cent

questions.q: Describe a situation (four or five lines) in which a king performs the ashvamedha yajna but his claim to be the most powerful ruler is NOT settled by the horse's journey alone. Use the rules of the ritual in your account.
questions.a: The horse wanders with soldiers across several lands; a neighbouring ruler stops it. Under the ritual this leads to a battle to determine supremacy, so the claim is settled only by the result of that battle, not by the wandering. Lands crossed without challenge before that still counted as part of the empire.
s: Horse wanders with soldiers and is stopped by a ruler
A stopped horse leads to a battle
The battle, not the journey, decides supremacy

questions.q: Which piece of evidence from the Shunga age best shows that the revival of Vedic rituals did not shut out other schools of thought?
questions.a: The Shungas added railings and reliefs about the Buddha's life at the Bharhut Stupa, Buddhist art made during a Vedic revival. The horse's route, the map and the language do not show other schools flourishing.
o: Buddha-life reliefs added at Bharhut
The route taken by the ashvamedha horse
The map showing the Shunga empire's extent
The language of the Yoga Sutras

questions.q: Was Pushyamitra Shunga a successful ruler? Give two points from the chapter that support calling him successful and one that goes against it.
questions.a: For: he kept the empire safe from potential invaders; he kept friendly relations with the Greeks after an initial campaign; he established himself as most powerful through the ashvamedha. Against: his empire was smaller than the Maurya empire and did not last long after him.
s: Two supporting points
One point against

questions.q: The chapter's collage of Shunga art includes bronze bangles covered with a thin layer of gold, a comb of ivory, beads of a necklace and a terracotta woman with hair ornaments. State two things historians can infer about the people of that time, naming the object each inference comes from.
questions.a: Any two with objects named, for example: gold-covered bronze bangles suggest craftworkers could plate metal and that people wore ornaments; the ivory comb suggests ivory was worked and that people cared about grooming; the beads and hair ornaments suggest that jewellery was commonly worn and made.
s: First inference tied to a named object
Second inference tied to a different object

questions.q: A student writes, 'Sanskrit works like the Yoga Sutras show the Shungas supported only Vedic learning.' (a) For what kinds of work does the chapter say Sanskrit was preferred? (b) Give one fact from the chapter showing that Shunga patronage went beyond Vedic matters.
questions.a: (a) Philosophical and literary works. (b) The Shungas added carved railings and reliefs on the Buddha's life at the Bharhut Stupa (also: they patronised art and architecture).
s: Philosophical and literary works
A fact showing patronage beyond Vedic matters, such as Bharhut

questions.q: The chapter prints a 19th-century painting of King Rama performing the ashvamedha yajna. A student argues, 'So the Shungas must have been the first to perform this ritual.' What is wrong with her argument?
questions.a: The chapter says the ritual was a Vedic one conducted by many rulers, and the painting is a 19th-century picture of a Ramayana scene, so it cannot show who first performed it or that the Shungas did. The other options state things the chapter does not say.
o: Many rulers conducted it; the painting does not show who began it
The ritual was meant only for kings of the Deccan, not of the north
The painting shows the Bharhut Stupa and not a ritual at all
The Shungas performed it only after the Mauryas had banned it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Shungas' revival of Vedic rituals meant that other schools of thought stopped flourishing in their lands.
Reason (R): The Shungas added carved railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life to the Bharhut Stupa.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says that although Vedic rituals and practices were revived, other schools of thought continued to flourish. R is true and is in fact evidence against A.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A museum label says, 'The Shunga empire ruled north and central India until about 20 BCE.' Use the chapter's dates to show that this cannot be correct.
questions.a: The chapter dates the assassination of the last Maurya emperor, after which Pushyamitra founded the dynasty, to around 185 BCE and says the empire was gone a century later, about 85 BCE. 20 BCE is about 65 years after that, so the empire had ended long before the label's date; the label overstates its life by more than half.
s: Starts from about 185 BCE
Works out about 85 BCE for the end
Shows 20 BCE is too late and corrects the label

questions.q: A king releases an ashvamedha horse with soldiers. It crosses the lands of Rulers P, Q and R. P and Q let it pass; R's soldiers stop it. Which conclusion about the three lands does the chapter's description of the ritual support?
questions.a: The chapter says any territory the horse crossed unchallenged was considered part of the king's empire, while a ruler who stopped the horse caused a battle to determine supremacy. So P's and Q's lands count, and R's is a matter for battle.
o: P's and Q's lands count as his; R's challenge leads to a battle for supremacy
Only R's land counts, because R alone dared to test the king's claim in battle
All three lands count, because the horse was escorted by the king's soldiers across each
None of the three lands counts until the horse has returned safely to the capital

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. A ruler's soldiers block the wandering horse  2. The horse crosses a border and no one challenges it  3. Railings of the Buddha's life are added in a reign that also performs a Vedic sacrifice  4. The Shunga king keeps the peace with the Greeks after one earlier clash
Column B: a. Vedic practice revived while other schools flourished  b. A battle to determine supremacy  c. Friendly relations kept after some initial campaign  d. The land counts as part of the king's empire
questions.a: Soldiers blocking the horse lead to a battle for supremacy; unchallenged crossing makes the land part of the empire; Buddhist reliefs added during a Vedic revival show that other schools flourished; peace after one earlier clash is friendly relations after an initial campaign.

questions.q:
Statement I: Pushyamitra performed the ashvamedha yajna to establish himself as a most powerful ruler.
Statement II: The Shunga empire outlived Pushyamitra by several centuries.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Statement I is true: the chapter gives that purpose. Statement II is false: the chapter says the empire did not last long after him and that a century later it was gone.
o: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Both statements are true.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are false.

questions.q:
Statement I: Though the Satavahana kings were devout followers of Vasudeva, they often granted tax-free agricultural land to Vedic scholars and to Jaina and Buddhist monks.
Statement II: The Karla caves, to which the Satavahanas contributed, were made for Buddhist monks.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Both are in the chapter: the kings followed Vasudeva yet patronised other schools with tax-free land grants, and the Karla caves near Lonavala were made for Buddhist monks.
o: Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are false.

questions.q: A historian wants to know why Gautamiputra Satakarni carried his mother's name. Which source in the chapter helps most directly?
questions.a: The chapter shows a coin with the Brahmi legend 'King Lord Satakarni, son of Gautami' alongside the statement that princes were often named after their mothers. The caves and the yaksha speak of monks, tolls and craftsmen, not naming.
o: A coin whose legend reads 'King Lord Satakarni, son of Gautami'
The Karla caves, made for Buddhist monks near Lonavala in Maharashtra
The Naneghat caves, used for collecting tolls and taxes near Pune
The Pitalkhora yaksha, with a goldsmith's name carved on its hand

questions.q: A museum has two Satavahana sources: coins with ships found from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh, and the Naneghat caves, which stood close to a major trade route near Pune and were used for collecting tolls and taxes. Which conclusion do the two sources support together, though neither supports it alone?
questions.a: The coins point to maritime trade across both coasts and the cave site shows tolls and taxes being collected on a trade route, so together they support trade as a source of revenue. The imports, the capitals and the monks are not shown by these two sources.
o: Trade by sea and by road brought the kingdom wealth and revenue
Glass and perfumed ointments were the kingdom's main imports
The capital moved from Amaravati to Paithan to be near the trade
Buddhist monks collected the tolls at the cave sites

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Satavahanas.
1. The Satavahana empire largely comprised present-day Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra, with different capital cities at different times.
2. Tolls and taxes added to the kingdom's revenue, and the Naneghat caves were used for collecting them as well as for resting places for traders.
3. Though devout followers of Vasudeva, the Satavahana kings also supported other schools of thought.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are in the chapter: the extent and the changing capitals, the revenue from tolls and taxes with the Naneghat caves, and the support for other schools despite devotion to Vasudeva.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Which inference from a Satavahana coin showing a two-masted ship is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says ships on coins suggest maritime trade mattered, the type of ship suggests advanced shipbuilding and navigation, and the wavy lines possibly represent water. It never says the kings commanded the ships.
o: Their kings commanded the trading ships
Maritime trade was important in economic life
Shipbuilding and navigation were advanced
The wavy lines may stand for ocean waters

questions.q: Why would the Satavahana kings have a toll post and resting caves at Naneghat? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: The caves lay close to a major trade route, so traders passed them; tolls and taxes on trade added to the kingdom's revenue and the caves were used to collect them; they also served as resting places for traders.
s: It lay close to a major trade route
Tolls and taxes for revenue, and rest for traders

questions.q: The Pitalkhora yaksha carries an inscription meaning 'made by Kanhadasa, a goldsmith'. A student writes, 'So in Satavahana times every stone sculptor was a goldsmith.' What is the most careful reading of the evidence?
questions.a: The inscription names one goldsmith who made a stone yaksha; the chapter only asks what this tells us about professions, so one example cannot prove a rule for all sculptors. The other options claim things the chapter does not say.
o: One goldsmith made a stone sculpture; one case cannot show what all craftsmen did
Goldsmiths were forbidden to carve stone, so the inscription must be a later addition by others
The yaksha was made of gold, which is why a goldsmith signed it
Sculptors had to train as goldsmiths before carving, as the chapter explains

questions.q: The Naneghat inscriptions in Brahmi include some numerals that, at times, resemble today's shapes. (a) What does the chapter conclude from this? (b) Why does the chapter call it only 'one of the many evidences' rather than proof by itself?
questions.a: (a) Modern numerals ultimately originated in India. (b) A few shapes in one set of inscriptions cannot settle the question alone; the conclusion rests on many pieces of evidence taken together, and only some of the numerals look like modern ones.
s: Modern numerals originated in India
One inscription is one piece among many evidences

questions.q:
A museum can display only one of two sources for its case on 'Royal women as patrons'. Source 1 is an inscription at Nashik that a powerful queen had carved. Source 2 is a set of inscriptions in caves near Pune, in Brahmi script, about a widow queen, listing gods and gifts.
(a) Name the queen of Source 1 and the prince named after her, and say why he carried her name.
(b) What had the queen of Source 1 donated?
(c) Name the Vedic ritual and two gods mentioned in Source 2, and the kinds of people who received her gifts.
(d) Choose one source for the case and name one thing your chosen source cannot tell visitors.
questions.a: (a) Gautami Balashri; her son Gautamiputra Satakarni, because princes were often named after their mothers. (b) Land to Buddhist monks. (c) The ashvamedha yajna (among several Vedic rituals); gods such as Indra, Chandra and Surya; gifts to priests, guests, workers, scholars and monks. (d) Either choice if reasoned: Source 1 shows a queen's influence in the kingdom but names one kind of recipient; Source 2 shows a wide range of gifts and rituals but does not name her influence in the same way. The limit named must be true of the chosen source.
s: Part (a): Gautami Balashri, Gautamiputra Satakarni and the naming custom
Part (b): land to Buddhist monks
Part (c): ashvamedha, two gods, and recipients
Part (d): a source chosen with one genuine limit

questions.q: (a) Name one thing that Gautami Balashri's gift and the Naneghat widow queen's gifts have in common and one thing in which they differ, according to the chapter. (b) Why can the historian not say from these two inscriptions alone that all Satavahana queens acted alike?
questions.a: (a) Common: both were royal women making donations that inscriptions record (Buddhist monks received gifts from both). Difference: Gautami Balashri gave land to Buddhist monks; the widow queen gave land, cows, horses, elephants and silver coins to priests, guests, workers, scholars and monks and performed Vedic rituals. (b) Two inscriptions are a small sample, so they show what these two women did, not what all queens did.
s: One similarity and one difference
Two cases are too few to show a general rule

questions.q: A museum guide tells visitors: 'The Satavahana kingdom's wealth came from sea trade with Rome, which is why the Naneghat caves were built to collect tolls from ships.' Which part does the chapter support and which part does it not?
questions.a: Partly right. Supported: the Satavahanas had trade networks reaching the Roman Empire and coins with ships show that maritime trade mattered. Not supported: the Naneghat caves stood near Pune close to a major trade route and were used for collecting tolls and taxes and as resting places for traders; the chapter does not say they were built for ships or that they were built for tolls.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: trade reaching Rome and ship coins
Not supported: Naneghat is an inland trade-route site used for tolls, not built to tax ships

questions.q: Write a museum label (three or four lines) for a Satavahana coin with a two-masted ship. The label must say what the coin suggests, what it shows about the kingdom's skills, and name one other source from the chapter that supports the same conclusion about trade.
questions.a: The coin suggests that maritime trade was an important part of economic life; the ship type suggests advanced shipbuilding and navigation; supporting source: the Naneghat caves where tolls and taxes were collected near a major trade route, or the record of goods exchanged with the Roman Empire.
s: Coin suggests maritime trade was important
Advanced shipbuilding and navigation
A second supporting source from the chapter

questions.q: Explain how farming, trade and a peaceful period together led to the Satavahana contribution to literature, art and culture. Show each link in the chain, name one site or object from the chapter as evidence of the contribution, and say which link the chapter supports least directly.
questions.a: Agriculture flourished in the Krishna-Godavari river system and gave economic stability. Trade, with coins, goods to and from the Roman Empire and tolls and taxes, added revenue. Prosperity and a relatively peaceful political period then facilitated the development of literature, art and culture. Evidence: the Karla caves made for Buddhist monks, or the Pitalkhora yaksha. The least direct link is between the prosperity and any particular site: the chapter states the general connection but does not tie each site to money from trade or farming.
s: Farming gave economic stability
Trade and tolls added revenue
Prosperity and a relatively peaceful period facilitated culture
One site or object as evidence
The least direct link, with a reason

questions.q: True or False: Among the Satavahanas, only kings are recorded as performing the ashvamedha yajna. Give the reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The Naneghat inscriptions record a Satavahana widow queen who, remarkably, performed several Vedic rituals including the ashvamedha yajna, and they list her gifts.
s: The verdict
The reason or correction

questions.q: A Satavahana coin shows a two-masted ship with wavy lines below. (a) What do the wavy lines possibly represent, and what does the type of ship suggest? (b) Why does finding such coins from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh strengthen the conclusion about trade?
questions.a: (a) The wavy lines possibly represent ocean waters; the type of ship suggests advanced shipbuilding and navigation. (b) The coins were found on both the western and eastern coasts, so seafaring trade mattered across the kingdom and not at one port alone.
s: Wavy lines as water and the ship suggesting advanced technology
Finds on both coasts show trade across the kingdom

questions.q:
Class 7 plans a 'Satavahana trade fair' for 300 visitors in 2 hours. Goods on the table: sandalwood, glass, ivory, perfumed ointments, textiles and spices. The class has Rs 3,000 for one display idea. Idea 1: a model of a cave on a trade route with a toll-counter game for 20 visitors at a time, 12 minutes a round, costing Rs 2,100. Idea 2: a printed card with a replica of a two-masted ship coin for every visitor, at Rs 9 each.
(a) How many of the six goods does the chapter name as imports? Name them.
(b) Work out how many visitors Idea 1 reaches in the 2 hours, and the money left under each idea.
(c) Which fact about the Satavahanas does each idea teach?
(d) Advise the class, weighing reach against depth.
questions.a: (a) Two: glass and perfumed ointments. (b) Idea 1: 120 / 12 = 10 rounds x 20 = 200 visitors, Rs 3,000 - 2,100 = Rs 900 left. Idea 2: 300 x 9 = Rs 2,700, Rs 300 left, all 300 reached. (c) Idea 1: tolls and taxes on trade added revenue (Naneghat on a trade route). Idea 2: ships on coins suggest maritime trade was important. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: Idea 2 reaches all 300 and leaves Rs 300 but is shallow; Idea 1 teaches by doing and leaves Rs 900 but 100 visitors miss the game.
s: Part (a): glass and perfumed ointments
Part (b): 200 visitors; Rs 900 and Rs 300
Part (c): tolls for Idea 1, maritime trade for Idea 2
Part (d): a choice weighing reach against depth

questions.q: A label says: 'The Satavahana empire, which ruled from the 2nd century BCE onward and fragmented in the 3rd century CE, lasted about 800 years.' Use the chapter's centuries to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The earliest the rule could begin is the first year of the 2nd century BCE (200 BCE) and the latest it could end is the last year of the 3rd century CE (300 CE). That is at most 200 + 300 = 500 years, which is less than 800, so the label cannot be right.
s: Earliest start 200 BCE and latest end 300 CE
Maximum of 500 years
500 is less than 800, so the label is wrong

questions.q:
Match each source in Column A with what it tells a historian in Column B.
Column A: 1. Coins showing ships  2. The Naneghat caves  3. A coin reading 'son of Gautami'  4. The inscription on the Pitalkhora yaksha
Column B: a. Naming after the mother  b. Maritime trade mattered  c. Tolls and rest at a trade route  d. A goldsmith also carved stone
questions.a: Ship coins suggest maritime trade; Naneghat was a toll and resting place near a trade route; the 'son of Gautami' legend shows naming after the mother; the Pitalkhora inscription shows a goldsmith making a stone sculpture.

questions.q: A clerk at the Naneghat toll post records 9 carts in an hour: 4 carry spices, 3 carry glass and 2 carry perfumed ointments. According to the chapter, ___ of the 9 carts carry goods named as imports.

Assertion (A): Literature, art and culture received significant contributions in the Satavahana kingdom.
Reason (R): Economic prosperity and a relatively peaceful political period facilitated such development.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter says prosperity and a relatively peaceful period made the development of literature, art and culture possible.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The Satavahana kingdom left behind coins, cave sites and inscriptions. Choose the ONE kind of source you think tells a historian most about life in the kingdom (not only trade) and defend your choice with three pieces of evidence from the chapter. Then say what one other kind of source adds.
questions.a: A strong answer chooses one source and supports it. For example, inscriptions: the Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri shows a powerful queen who donated land to Buddhist monks; the Naneghat inscriptions show a widow queen performing Vedic rituals including the ashvamedha and giving land, cows, horses and silver coins; the Brahmi numerals show early number symbols. Coins add the evidence of ships and maritime trade, and caves like Karla and Naneghat add patronage and toll collection. Accept any consistent choice.
s: Chooses one kind of source
First piece of evidence from the chapter
Second piece of evidence
Third piece of evidence
What another kind of source adds

questions.q: True or False: Kharavela was sometimes called bhikshu-raja, 'monk-king', so he had given up ruling to live as a monk. Give the reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says he was a devoted follower of Jain teachings and was called monk-king, but his inscription records his victorious military campaigns and works for his people's welfare, so he continued to rule.
s: The verdict
The reason or correction

questions.q: A student writes: 'Kalinga rose as a power under the Chedis before the Maurya empire declined.' Using the chapter, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says Kalinga rose as a prominent power after the decline of the Maurya empire, under the Chedi dynasty. The decline is the breakup that followed the assassination of the last emperor around 185 BCE, so a rise 'before the decline' puts the Chedis ahead of an event the chapter says came first. The order in the student's sentence is reversed.
s: Quotes the chapter: after the decline of the Maurya empire
The decline began with the breakup after the assassination around 185 BCE
Concludes the order is reversed and corrects it

questions.q: Write a short inscription (three lines) in Kharavela's own voice that is consistent with the chapter. It must include one deed of war, one work for the welfare of his people, and one line about how he treats faiths other than his own.
questions.a: A good inscription has a victorious campaign (the chapter mentions campaigns, for example an alliance of southern kings), a benevolent work for his people's welfare, and a line such as being a respector of every sect and a repairer of every temple. Wording is original; it must not claim anything the chapter denies, such as invading the south.
s: One victorious military campaign
One work for the welfare of the people
Respect for every sect

questions.q: The chapter wonders how artisans made rock-cut chambers so regular 'with just a chisel and a hammer'. (a) What does the regularity of the chambers show about the craftsmen, according to the chapter? (b) Why would a mistake be harder to correct in a rock-cut chamber than in a built wall?
questions.a: (a) The design and craftsmanship of the caves showcase the skill of the craftsmen. (b) Stone that has been cut away from the rock cannot be put back, so each cut had to be right (a reasoned answer along these lines is accepted).
s: Shows great skill of the craftsmen
Cut-away rock cannot be restored, so errors are costly

questions.q: A student separates Kharavela's own claims in the Hathigumpha inscription from statements made by the chapter's author. Which of these is a claim by Kharavela himself?
questions.a: The 'respector of every sect' description is quoted from the inscription as his own claim. The other three are the chapter's own statements about the caves, his southern campaign and the Chedis.
o: He is 'accomplished in extraordinary virtues, respector of every sect and repairer of every temple'
The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves are notable examples of what the chapter calls rock-cut architecture
According to the chapter, he does not seem to have invaded the southern region at any time
Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the kings of the Chedi dynasty after the decline of the Mauryas

questions.q: A museum label draft reads: 'The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were made for Jain monks.' (a) Which word in the chapter's own description shows the claim is not certain? (b) Rewrite the label so that it is faithful to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 'Likely': the chapter says the caves were likely developed for Jain monks. (b) For example: 'The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were likely developed for Jain monks.'
s: The word 'likely'
A rewritten label that keeps the hedge

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with what it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1. The Hathigumpha inscription  2. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves  3. Hundreds of pearls from the Pandya kingdom  4. The title bhikshu-raja
Column B: a. Kharavela's Jain devotion  b. A record of deeds year after year  c. Contact with the south  d. Rock-cut architecture
questions.a: The inscription records deeds year after year; the caves are rock-cut architecture; pearls from the Pandya kingdom point to contact with the south; bhikshu-raja reflects his Jain devotion.

questions.q: (a) Give one thing the Hathigumpha inscription tells a historian directly about Kharavela's reign. (b) Give one claim in it that the chapter says cannot be pinned down, and say why.
questions.a: (a) Any one: it records his accomplishments year after year, including victorious campaigns and welfare works; he created a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions. (b) His claim to have defeated an alliance of south Indian kings: the location of that battle is unknown and he does not seem to have invaded the south.
s: One thing recorded directly
The southern battle claim, with the reason

questions.q: (a) In which script is the Hathigumpha inscription written, and name two other records in the chapter that use it. (b) What does the use of one script in Kalinga and in the Deccan suggest?
questions.a: (a) Brahmi; for example the Satavahana coin legend 'King Lord Satakarni, son of Gautami' and the Naneghat inscriptions (also the inscription on Kanishka's statue). (b) That one script was in use across distant regions and under different dynasties.
s: Brahmi and two other records
A script shared across regions and dynasties

questions.q: Kharavela's inscription says hundreds of pearls were brought to him from the Pandya kingdom, while the chapter says he does not seem to have invaded the south. What does this combination suggest?
questions.a: The chapter states that he does not seem to have invaded the southern region, while the inscription records pearls being brought from the Pandya kingdom, which points to trade contact. Rule or tribute is not claimed by the chapter.
o: Trade contact rather than conquest
The Pandyas were ruled by Kalinga
Pearls were paid as tribute after a war in the south
The Pandya kingdom did not exist in his time

questions.q:
A museum wants a title for a panel on the Hathigumpha inscription. For a classroom exercise the teacher invents a translation with 8 yearly entries: 5 describe campaigns and 3 describe works for the people's welfare. Title 1: 'Kharavela the conqueror'. Title 2: 'Kharavela the protector of his people and of every faith'.
(a) To which dynasty did Kharavela belong, and what was he sometimes called?
(b) What percentage of the invented entries describe campaigns, and what percentage describe welfare?
(c) Which phrase in the real inscription supports the words 'of every faith' in Title 2?
(d) Which title would you choose? Use your percentages and the chapter, and say what the other title leaves out.
questions.a: (a) The Chedi dynasty; the monk-king (bhikshu-raja). (b) 5 / 8 = 62.5 per cent campaigns and 3 / 8 = 37.5 per cent welfare. (c) 'Respector of every sect and repairer of every temple'. (d) Either title can be defended: Title 1 matches the majority of the invented entries but omits welfare works and respect for all sects; Title 2 matches what the chapter stresses about his attitude but gives less weight to the 62.5 per cent of entries about war.
s: Part (a): Chedi dynasty; monk-king
Part (b): 62.5 and 37.5 per cent
Part (c): respector of every sect and repairer of every temple
Part (d): a title chosen, naming what the other leaves out

questions.q: The Satavahana section ends with the empire fragmenting in the 3rd century CE. The next section, on the Chedis, opens with 'Let us go back a little'. What makes the chapter go back in time?
questions.a: The chapter says that after the decline of the Maurya empire, which it dates from around 185 BCE, Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the Chedis. That is some four centuries before the Satavahana fragmentation in the 3rd century CE, so the chapter goes back. The Chedi rise came after, not before, the Mauryas and the Kalinga war.
o: Kalinga rose after the Maurya decline of the 2nd century BCE, long before the 3rd century CE
Kharavela ruled before Ashoka and before the Kalinga war that the previous chapter described
The Chedis were an older dynasty than the Mauryas and ruled Kalinga before them
Kalinga's rise as a power followed the fragmentation of the Satavahana empire in the 3rd century CE

questions.q:
Statement I: The Hathigumpha inscription, written in Pali script, records only Kharavela's victories in war.
Statement II: After the Maurya empire declined, Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the Chedi dynasty.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Statement I is false on two counts: the inscription is in Brahmi script and it records his welfare works as well as his victorious campaigns. Statement II is in the chapter.
o: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Both statements are false.

questions.q:
A class visits the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar for 120 minutes. The guide says that one cave prominently displays a famous inscription. Plan A: spend 20 minutes at each of 5 caves, one of them the inscription cave. Plan B: spend 60 minutes at the inscription cave and 15 minutes at each of 4 other caves.
(a) For whom were these caves likely developed, and in which script is the inscription written?
(b) Work out the time each plan uses and the time left unused.
(c) Which two kinds of achievement would visitors read about at the inscription cave?
(d) Which plan would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Jain monks (likely); Brahmi script. (b) Plan A: 5 x 20 = 100 minutes, 20 minutes unused. Plan B: 60 + 4 x 15 = 120 minutes, none unused. (c) Victorious military campaigns and benevolent works for the welfare of his people. (d) Either plan if justified: Plan B gives an hour to read the inscription's campaigns and welfare works but leaves no slack and sees fewer caves for long; Plan A sees all five caves and the range of rock-cut work, with 20 minutes spare.
s: Part (a): Jain monks (likely) and Brahmi
Part (b): 100 minutes with 20 spare; 120 minutes with none
Part (c): campaigns and welfare works
Part (d): a plan chosen with a reason from the inscription or the caves

questions.q:
Read the statements about Kharavela and the Chedis.
1. The Hathigumpha inscription, written in Brahmi script, records Kharavela's accomplishments year after year.
2. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves lie near Pune, close to a major trade route, and were used to collect tolls.
3. Kharavela says he created a council of ascetics and sages drawn only from Kalinga.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the caves are near Bhubaneswar, and the cave near Pune on a trade route is Naneghat. Statement 3 is false: the council was from a hundred regions.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves are notable examples of rock-cut architecture.
Reason (R): The chambers there were built up by joining cut stone blocks into rooms and panels.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true and R is false: the chapter describes panels, statues and spacious rooms carved into the rock itself, which is why the caves count as rock-cut architecture.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A guide mixes up two cave sites from the chapter. Which statement about them is correct?
questions.a: The chapter says the Karla caves near Lonavala were made for Buddhist monks and the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were likely developed for Jain monks. The tolls and trade route belong to the Naneghat caves near Pune.
o: Karla, near Lonavala, was made for Buddhist monks; Udayagiri-Khandagiri, near Bhubaneswar, was likely for Jain monks
Karla, near Bhubaneswar, was made for Jain monks; Udayagiri-Khandagiri, near Lonavala, was made for Buddhist monks
Both Karla and Udayagiri-Khandagiri were likely developed for Jain monks, and both lie near Bhubaneswar
Karla was used to collect tolls near Pune on a trade route; Udayagiri-Khandagiri was made for Buddhist monks

questions.q: Prepare a five-point information board for visitors to the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves that is faithful to the chapter. It must cover where the caves are and their kind of architecture, what the Hathigumpha inscription is and records, Kharavela's faith and attitude to others, how Kalinga came to rise, and one statement that visitors should be told is uncertain, with the reason.
questions.a: Point 1: caves near Bhubaneswar, rock-cut architecture with panels, statues and rooms carved into rock. Point 2: the Hathigumpha inscription in Brahmi script records Kharavela's accomplishments year after year, campaigns and welfare works. Point 3: he was a devoted Jain, called monk-king, who respected every sect. Point 4: after the decline of the Maurya empire, Kalinga rose as a power under the Chedi dynasty. Point 5: the caves were only 'likely' developed for Jain monks, or the location of his southern battle is unknown.
s: Place and rock-cut architecture
Inscription: script and what it records
Faith and respect for all sects
Kalinga's rise under the Chedis after the Maurya decline
One uncertain statement with its reason

questions.q: Use the Hathigumpha inscription to explain how a historian should use a ruler's own record. Say what it tells us directly, why its statements about the ruler need care, what the chapter says about one claim that cannot be placed, and what other evidence in the chapter helps check the ruler's relation with the south.
questions.a: Directly: it is in Brahmi and records his deeds year after year, campaigns and welfare works, and describes him as a respector of every sect. Care: it is the king's own account, so it praises him. The claim that he defeated an alliance of south Indian kings has no known location, and he does not seem to have invaded the south. Other evidence: the same inscription mentions hundreds of pearls brought from the Pandya kingdom, which suggests trade contact; Ashoka's edicts show the south stayed independent. Conclusion: use the record, but check each claim against other sources.
s: What the inscription records directly
Why a ruler's own record needs care
The unplaced southern battle and no invasion
Pearls from the Pandyas as other evidence of contact
A conclusion on how to use such a source

questions.q: A letter in the school magazine claims: 'Kharavela's inscription shows that he protected only Jain sages and Jain temples, since he was a devoted Jain.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Kharavela was a devoted follower of Jain teachings, but in the inscription he calls himself a 'respector of every sect and repairer of every temple', and says he created a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions. The chapter reads this as a ruler taking pride in protecting all schools of thought.
s: Verdict: No
The quotation 'respector of every sect and repairer of every temple'
The council of a hundred regions or the chapter's reading as protection of all schools

questions.q: The chapter says the Chola king Karikala 'is said to have defeated a combined force of the Cheras and Pandyas and established his supremacy'. Which reading is supported by this sentence?
questions.a: 'Combined force' means the two rival kingdoms fought together against Karikala, and he is said to have beaten them and established his supremacy. The chapter does not say they were one kingdom, allies of the Cholas, or that their dynasties ended; it says the three often competed.
o: The Cheras and Pandyas had joined forces against the Cholas and still lost
The Cheras and Pandyas had always been a single kingdom until this defeat in battle
The Cheras and Pandyas were allies of the Cholas in this battle

o: The titles are his own proclamation; his empire reached from central Asia to large parts of northern India
The titles are a later addition, since the chapter says the statue is headless and damaged
The titles prove nothing about his power; they only show that he followed the Buddha
The titles are right, because the chapter says the Kushanas ruled the whole subcontinent and beyond

questions.q: Describe two imagined sculptures, one in the Gandhara style and one in the Mathura style, in a sentence each, so that a classmate could tell them apart. Mention stone, the look of the figure and a subject in each sentence.
questions.a: Gandhara: carved in grey-black schist, a Buddha with realistic anatomy and flowing robes, showing Greco-Roman touches with Indian features. Mathura: carved in red sandstone, a full, smoothly modelled figure of an Indian deity such as Kubera, Lakshmi, Shiva, yakshas or yakshinis, with less Greco-Roman influence.
s: Gandhara sentence with stone and look
Mathura sentence with stone and look
A suitable subject in each

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mathura sculptures show less Greco-Roman influence than Gandhara sculptures.
Reason (R): Mathura sculptures were carved mainly in red sandstone.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the stone does not explain the difference in influence: the chapter gives the Mathura style's distinct Indian character as the reason, and the material is simply another difference.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The chapter says that despite political conflicts and power struggles the period saw remarkable cultural exchange. (a) Name one way, from the chapter, in which this exchange shows in the Kushana age. (b) What does the chapter conclude about how we should view the 'Tapestry of the Past'?
questions.a: (a) Any one: the fusion of Indian and Greek styles in Gandhara and Mathura art; Buddha and Shiva on coins; the variety of deities in sculpture; Sanskrit literature and the major epics. (b) Not as confined to any one kingdom or ruler but as a dynamic process through interaction and assimilation over time.
s: One example of exchange
A dynamic process of interaction, not one kingdom or ruler

questions.q: Two Buddha statues are on display. One is in red sandstone with a full, smoothly modelled figure; the other is in grey-black schist with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. A visitor says the red sandstone statue shows more Greco-Roman influence. What is the correct reading?
questions.a: The chapter says Gandhara sculptors used grey-black schist and blended Greco-Roman elements with Indian features, with realistic anatomy and flowing robes; Mathura sculptors used red sandstone, made fuller smooth figures and reflect less Greco-Roman influence.
o: No; the schist one is Gandhara-style with more Greco-Roman influence, while red sandstone points to Mathura's Indian style
No; the red sandstone statue shows Greek influence only because Mathura sculptors had come from Greece itself
Yes; red sandstone was the stone of the Gandhara school, which blended Greco-Roman and Indian features
Yes; the full figure and smooth modelling are the marks of a school with strong Greco-Roman influence

questions.q: A student sees one Kanishka coin with the Buddha and another with Shiva beside the bull Nandi and says, 'He must have given up one faith for the other.' Which reading is closer to the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter asks what putting the Buddha and Shiva on his coins says about his values, and notes that the sculptures of the age reflect the peaceful co-existence of various schools of thought. The other options bring in Kharavela, a script the chapter does not name for the coin and land grants of the Satavahanas.
o: The coins and the sculptures of the age point to peaceful co-existence of schools of thought
The coins show that he followed Jain teachings, as Kharavela of Kalinga did
The coins show that the Buddha's name was written in Brahmi script to please local priests
The coins show that he gave tax-free agricultural land to monks of every school

questions.q: A coin of a dynasty that came from central Asia shows the Buddha with his name in Greek script. (a) What does the Greek script suggest about the cultures that reached the Kushanas? (b) Which earlier foreign rulers in the northwest set the trend that Kushana art continued?
questions.a: (a) That Greek influence was still present, as part of the cultural intermixing and fusion of Indian and Greek styles in Kushana times. (b) The Indo-Greek rulers.
s: Greek influence and fusion of styles
Indo-Greek rulers set the trend

questions.q:
A school is setting up a room on the Kushana age with 40 square metres of floor. Proposal 1 is a wall display on the Silk Route and trade, needing 24 square metres. Proposal 2 is a sculpture corner placing Gandhara and Mathura pieces side by side, needing 18 square metres.
(a) How much space do the two proposals need together, and by how much does that exceed the room?
(b) What does the chapter say the Kushana hold on sections of the Silk Route did for trade?
(c) What does the chapter say about how the Gandhara and Mathura schools differ in their stone?
(d) The school can trim 2 square metres from only one proposal. Which would you trim, and why?
questions.a: (a) 24 + 18 = 42 square metres, which is 2 more than 40. (b) Trade grew, connecting India with other parts of Asia and the West. (c) Gandhara used grey-black schist; Mathura used red sandstone. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: trimming the Silk Route wall keeps both schools side by side so the contrast and the fusion can be seen; trimming the sculpture corner keeps the trade story, which is the chapter's other main development of the age.
s: Part (a): 42 square metres, 2 over
Part (b): trade grew, connecting India with Asia and the West
Part (c): grey-black schist and red sandstone
Part (d): a trimming choice with a reason from the chapter

questions.q: A museum describes three artefacts. (A) A standing Buddha in grey-black schist with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. (B) A fuller, smoothly modelled yakshini in red sandstone. (C) A coin showing Kanishka with a spear, and the Buddha labelled in Greek script. For each artefact say which school or kind of evidence it belongs to and one thing it shows about the Kushana age. Then say what the three together show.
questions.a: A belongs to the Gandhara school: it shows the fusion of Greco-Roman elements with Indian features. B belongs to the Mathura school: a distinct Indian style with Indian deities such as yakshas and yakshinis. C is a coin of Kanishka: it shows the Buddha named in Greek script, so the cultural intermixing, and the king's respect for more than one faith. Together they show cultural fusion and co-existence, with Indian themes remaining strong, which is why the chapter calls the period a dynamic process of interaction and assimilation.
s: A: Gandhara and its Greco-Roman blend
B: Mathura and its Indian style and subjects
C: coin with Greek-script Buddha
What the three show together: fusion and co-existence

questions.q:
Statement I: Gandhara sculptors made fine Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes, working mainly in grey-black schist.
Statement II: Mathura sculptures generally show fuller figures with smooth modelling and reflect less Greco-Roman influence than Gandhara.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter: Gandhara used grey-black schist and produced realistic Buddha images, and Mathura used red sandstone, made fuller figures with smooth modelling and showed less Greco-Roman influence.
o: Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are false.

questions.q: One of the sculptures in the chapter shows a Naga between two Nagis and carries an inscription that refers to the eighth year of Kanishka's reign. What can a historian conclude from the inscription alone?
questions.a: An inscription that refers to a king's regnal year dates the object to his reign, here the eighth year of Kanishka. It does not say who carved it, who ruled whom, or anything about a change of his faith.
o: The sculpture dates to the Kushana period, to the eighth year of Kanishka's reign
Kanishka carved the sculpture himself in the eighth year of his reign
The Nagas ruled the Kushanas until the eighth year of Kanishka's reign
Kanishka gave up the Buddha for the Nagas in his eighth year

questions.q: In a peer-marked test, a classmate's answer is 'Kanishka was a Buddhist ruler.' How far does the chapter support this? Give evidence for the part that is supported and the part that goes too far.
questions.a: Supported to a degree: one of his coins shows the Buddha with the name BODDO in Greek script. It goes too far if it means only Buddhism: another coin shows Shiva with the bull Nandi, and Kushana sculptures show many deities, reflecting peaceful co-existence of schools of thought.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: Buddha on a coin
Too far: Shiva with Nandi and many deities in sculpture

questions.q: Which of the three foreign peoples in this chapter, the Indo-Greeks, the Shakas or the Kushanas, changed life in the subcontinent the most? Defend your choice with two pieces of evidence and say what each of the other two added.
questions.a: A strong answer chooses one and supports it. Kushanas: control of significant sections of the Silk Route, so trade grew; the Gandhara and Mathura schools; Buddha and Shiva on coins; human-like deities that laid groundwork for temples. Indo-Greeks added a blend of Greek and Indian elements and coins with Indian deities, and the Heliodorus pillar. The Shakas added the Shaka Samvat calendar, developed during their period and adopted as the Indian National Calendar in 1957. Accept any consistent choice.
s: Chooses one people
First piece of evidence
Second piece of evidence
What one of the other two added
What the third added

questions.q: The chapter says the Kushanas entered India probably in the 2nd century CE. Counting from the last year of that century to the year 2026, they had entered at least ___ years earlier.

Read the statements about the Kushana age.
1. The Kushanas held significant sections of the Silk Route, which let them dominate all trade between China and the Mediterranean.
2. The Gandhara style emerged in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh.
3. The sculptures of the Kushana age show a variety of deities, which the chapter reads as reflecting peaceful co-existence of various schools of thought.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 goes too far: the chapter says the Kushanas held significant sections and that trade grew, connecting India with other parts of Asia and the West, not that they dominated all trade. Statement 2 is false: Gandhara emerged in the western regions of Punjab. Statement 3 is in the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) Where did the Gandhara style emerge, and where did the Mathura style develop? (b) Why could both schools flourish under one dynasty, according to the extent of the Kushana empire?
questions.a: (a) Gandhara in the western regions of Punjab; Mathura in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh. (b) The empire extended from central Asia to large parts of northern India, so both regions lay within one empire (a reasoned answer: ideas and craftsmen could move between them).
s: Both regions correctly placed
Both lay within one large northern empire

questions.q: True or False: A Kushana coin could carry the name of an Indian figure written in Greek script. Give the reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. On one of Kanishka's coins the Buddha appears with the inscription BODDO in Greek script, an example of the fusion of Indian and Greek elements in Kushana times.
s: The verdict
The reason or correction
